newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Lord Hanson annoints Collins as successor.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Lord Hanson annoints Collins as successor.

text.p: LONDON, May 15 (Reuter) Once-mighty conglomerate Hanson Plc, which ended an era with the completion of a four-way demerger in February, flagged another new beginning on Thursday when it said founder Lord Hanson will be succeeded as chairman by Chris Collins.
Lord Hanson will retire at the end of this year and be appointed chairman emeritus like fellow British industrial icon Lord Weinstock, former chief of GEC Plc.
But unlike GEC, Lord Hanson's successor is a company and family insider who has pledged to continue with the strategy he has inherited.
Christopher Collins, who is married to Lord Hanson's niece and is still deputy chairman, told Reuters: "I am totally committed to the new Hanson strategy."
Lord Hanson announced the demerger last year after the group became one of the worst performing stocks in the FTSE 100 index of leading UK shares.
The move shook the corporate establishment. After 45 years of building the international giant, Lord Hanson unveiled a strategy to dismantle his life's work.
The group saw Imperial Tobacco Plc and Millennium Chemicals demerging in October, with the process completed when Energy Group Plc was spun off earlier this year.
New Hanson now only consists of the rump building group which spans materials to construction in Britain, the Continent and the U.S.
"Our future development will be in building materials and construction through capital expenditure and bolt-ons (acquisitions)," summed up Collins who started off with the group in Australia.
"We see the U.S. as a big area of opportunity and obviously we have a substantial interest in developing within Europe."
He said Lord Hanson would not stay on as a back-seat driver consultant, but would be available to give his advice from time to time.
The title of chairman emeritus "honours his enormous contribution", said Collins.
Before taking on the deputy chairmanship, Collins was corporate affairs director for the pre-demerger group.
He comes from a chartered accounting background and started his working life at the family perfume business Goya where he was chief executive.
British-based Goya has since been bought by Imperial Chemical Industries Plc.

The announcement of the succession came on the day new Hanson unveiled its first half pretax profits. The headline figure was distorted by the inclusion of a five-month constribution from the now demerged Energy Group and other exceptionals.
The pretax profit figure for the first half to March 31 was 262.8 million pounds ($431.7 million), with no meaningful comparison for the year before the split.

Collins said the true picture of new Hanson's performance lay in the operating profit for continuing operations. That stood at 69.6 million versus 66.3 million previously. No dividend is payable this period.

Lord Hanson was upbeat about the fortunes of the FTSE 100 building group. "The signs of improvement in the UK housing and construction markets are now more evident, the prospects for our U.S. businesses are good and we look forward to making steady progress during the rest of 1997," he said.
He added that group was in "excellent shape to build value for shareholders."
But the shares remained depressed, losing seven pence to 322 by 1415 GMT.

The group saw profits move ahead at most units, with ARC up to 30.7 million from 28.9 million pounds. Cornerstone profits up to 3.9 million from 2.7 million; Hanson Brick profits rose to 12.9 million from 9.8 million but Grover Worldwide fell to 20.9 million from 22.9 million.

The results included 8.9 million in profit from a stake in an Australian mining business, 5.9 million in profit from the now-sold Hanson Electrical and 238.8 million from the five-month Energy contribution. ($ = 0.608 British Pounds)
